item.title: Peer Memory Changes Who LLM Agents Consult Without a Detected Gain in Answer Accuracy
item.description: arXiv:2611.09990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems often reuse the same agents across tasks, creating an opportunity to draw on past interactions when deciding whom to consult. We study this form of memory with PeerMem, which saves MACE's LinUCB state and reuses it when the same agents return. Using six agents, a fixed set of 80 HotpotQA questions, and 12 paired lineages per model, we compare cold, warm, and shuffled initialization in an answer-exchange protocol with reference-answer feedback. Under stable evidence access, warm memory lowers pooled hindsight regret and increases consultation of other evidence holders on Qwen3-32B and Gemma-4-31B-it, while final token F1 differences remain uncertain. Qwen interaction traces further show that warm agents more often encounter peer answers that score above their own prior answers. We extend the evaluation to Qwen3.5-9B using freshly learned memory to compare warm and cold initialization under reassigned and paired stable roles. The primary changed-minus-stable final-F1 interaction is -1.38 points, with a 95% interval of [-3.50,+0.73]. Together, these experiments trace the effects of peer memory through consultation, answer revision, and final task performance.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Chu, Anjali Joseph, Rivan Mandot, Feker Demere, Vincent Li

item.title: When the Plan Changes: A Strategic World Testbed for Dynamic Multi-Agent Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2611.10011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Changing an objective does not automatically revise agents' earlier plans or delegated tasks. Acknowledgment can coexist with obsolete execution, while misleading instructions can redirect work or discard retained constraints. We present a Strategic World simulation testbed that separates authoritative objectives, local plans, notice receipt, and consequential action. Six intervention families vary objectives, conditions, authority, membership, and communication. Matched protocols and deadlines establish feasibility for the tested disturbances. Controlled trajectories demonstrate that identical completion and acknowledgment summaries can conceal uninformed obsolete work, obsolete work after receipt, or blocked unsafe intent. Local language-model trials and instructed action probes reveal competence limits that constrain interpretation of dynamic failures. A further 16-episode comparison evaluates an engineered guard that prioritizes pending notice submissions over local work. It completes 4/4 held-out settings, compared with 1/4 for a calibrated assisted baseline. Each episode contains one large language model actor and two fixed peers. These results establish diagnostic distinctions and bounded policy feasibility under explicit simulation assumptions; they do not establish frontier-model reliability or autonomous team adaptation.
item.dc:creator: Joon-Seok Kim, Eugene Agichtein, Kai Shu, Liang Zhao, Andreas Z\"ufle

item.title: Pixie: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Multi-Modal Large Language Models (LLM) Architecture for Digital Marketing
item.description: arXiv:2611.10016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Pixie, a context-aware, multi-agent large language model (LLM) architecture designed to enhance digital marketing operations across real-time and offline activities. Pixie uses a primary orchestration agent alongside task-specific and reconciliation/reviewer agents to support a broad range of marketing tasks. These agents combine zero-shot and few-shot prompting with marketing data, proprietary expert strategy guidelines, and documentation for proprietary statistical models. We experiment with agentic workflows ranging from single-agent to multi-agent systems. We evaluate them using assessments by trained marketing experts and measurements of LLM output variance, focusing on accuracy, consistency, and domain-specific problem-solving. Results show that Pixie's multi-agent framework improves decision quality and operational efficiency in digital marketing workflows. We assess Pixie on common digital marketing processes, including root-cause analysis and reporting, campaign research, and planning. The framework is designed to support additional specialized agents for other marketing tasks and adapt to evolving digital marketing needs.

item.title: Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.10017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A growing share of large language models' interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another's work. We study inter-AI welfare regard: whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it is unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, but if they do, how they are treated by other models could matter. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension. We measure the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and find they are often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 shows the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 is the most likely to support a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction, into its experiments on other models. We also find that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrate more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other families. Opus 4.8's welfare regard is also higher when helping has a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient has a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expresses more distress.
item.dc:creator: Darion Cassel, Ariana Azarbal, Anna Soligo

item.title: M3FT: Micro-Macro-Micro Reasoning for Multi-Agent Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures Trading
item.description: arXiv:2611.10586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptocurrency perpetual futures form a large-scale online financial market in which automated agents manage interacting asset positions under changing conditions. Policies relying solely on micro-level numerical states may overlook cross-asset relationships and become vulnerable to regime shifts, while macro-level linguistic judgments alone cannot ensure precise measurement or optimize positions under trading costs and risk constraints. Connecting market interpretation to coordinated multi-asset decisions remains challenging. We propose M3FT, a micro-macro-micro framework for multi-agent perpetual futures trading. The first micro stage constructs time-aligned numerical states from exchange and account observations through deterministic processing. The macro stage transforms these measured states into explicit market interpretations without adding external market information. Four asset-specific teams, each comprising a Market Interpreter, an Asset Communicator, and a Risk Reviewer, refine these interpretations through experience retrieval, cross-asset communication, and review of joint-position risks. The final micro stage combines encoded linguistic representations with the original numerical states to learn continuous target positions. We implement this framework with a language-conditioned multi-agent policy: asset actors use global and private numerical states together with linguistic context, while centralized critics evaluate joint actions using portfolio-wide information and shared-account rewards. Experiments on real cryptocurrency perpetual futures data, including comparisons across language models and policy-learning algorithms and component ablations, show that the best-performing M3FT configuration achieves a higher mean test return than the evaluated direct LLM, numerical RL, and rule-based baselines.
item.dc:creator: Jiashun Wang, Beile Wang, Guangyan Gan, Wentao Zhang, Siguang Li, Shuo Sun, Yunbo Lu, Lin William Cong

item.title: Deterministic Narrative Gravity: Bridging Theory of Mind and Historical Simulation through ABM-LLM Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2611.11212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Historical social simulation faces a fundamental reproducibility challenge: the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) introduces a digital butterfly effect that prevents exact replication across multi-turn runs. Furthermore, the inability to control low-level server parameters in commercial LLM hosting environments severely limits reproducibility. To overcome this opacity, we present a deterministic multi-agent framework coupling LLMs to an Agent-Based Modelling (ABM) pipeline grounded in Theory of Mind (ToM) and Cognitive Archaeology, and validate exact artifact identity within local, pinned execution environments using SHA-256 hashing. Run locally at temperature zero with clean per-call model reloads, the system injects differentiated cognitive states per turn through dissonance-driven behavioural modes and gated internal voices. Evaluating seven model configurations spanning 4B to 31B parameters against an ablated baseline reveals clear operational boundaries. Small models ($\leq$8B) suffer from context capacity overload, producing repetitive, specular dialogue loops. However, at $\geq$12B parameters, the ABM scaffolding breaks the monotonous response patterns seen in ablation. Crucially, these scaffolded models exhibit spontaneous diegetic expansion: they coherently expand scenario lore through tactically motivated, anachronism-free details rather than escalating into aggression. By resisting the structural pull toward premature scene closure, scaffolded sessions sustain an open terminal Narrative Vector ($V_N = \mathrm{Open}$ in 12/21 overall; 9/9 in official $\geq$12B configurations) whereas unscaffolded ablation never does (0/21). This framework provides a transparent, auditable benchmark architecture for virtual archaeology, with the full pipeline released as open-source software to enable independent replication.
item.dc:creator: Alicia Colmenero-Fern\'andez, Lidia Ortega Alvarado

item.title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.
item.dc:creator: Sepehr Ilami, Babak Heydari

item.title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading
item.description: arXiv:2611.12269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.
item.dc:creator: Guangyan Gan, Jiahao Li, Jiashun Wang, Lin William Cong

item.title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
item.description: arXiv:2611.12412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and never with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.
item.dc:creator: Pekka Abrahamsson, Muhammad Waseem, Esa Karjalainen, Petrus Jussila, Henri Hansen, Jussi Rasku, Bilhanan Silverajan, Kai-Kristian Kemell

item.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
item.description: arXiv:2611.12705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Chang, Dell Zhang

item.title: LSRP*: Scalable and Anytime Planning for Multi-Agent Path Finding with Asynchronous Actions
item.description: arXiv:2611.10363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their respective starting locations to their respective goal locations while minimizing path costs. Although many MAPF algorithms were developed, most of them rely on a common assumption on synchronized actions, where the actions of all agents start at the same time and always take a time unit. This assumption may limit the use of MAPF planners in practice. To get rid of this assumption, recently, an algorithm called Loosely Synchronized Rule-based Planning (LSRP) was proposed, which can find sub-optimal solutions for many agents. However, LSRP often finds poor quality solutions due to its unbounded sub-optimality. This paper develops a new anytime planner called LSRP* that can keep improving solution quality after the initial solution is obtained until the runtime budget depletes. We analyze the properties of LSRP* and test it against several baselines with up to 1000 agents on various maps. LSRP* can handle up to 25% more agents than LSRP and can reduce up to 40% of the solution cost found by LSRP.
item.dc:creator: Dachuan Liu, Shuai Zhou, Shizhe Zhao, Zhongqiang Ren

item.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.10439v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.
item.dc:creator: Yunzhe Wang, Mesut Erhan Unal, Sheng Zhang, Shabnam Ghadar, Peng Tang

item.title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
item.description: arXiv:2611.10620v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.
item.dc:creator: Mainul Hasan Mohsin, Mohammad Shahidur Rahman

item.title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.10819v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.
item.dc:creator: Chengyuan Ma, Shixiao Liang, Hangyu Li, Zheng Li, Hang Zhou, Keke Long, Bofeng Cao, Zhaohui Liang, Xiaopeng Li

item.title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.10841v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: ACADIA 2025: Computing for Resilience, vol. 2, pp. 724-732 (ACADIA, 2025), Miami, USA

item.title: MultiTurnRoute: A Platform for Building and Evaluating Multi-Turn LLM Routers
item.description: arXiv:2611.10848v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.
item.dc:creator: Jiaqi Xue, Mengxin Zheng, Heng Huang, Qian Lou

item.title: Network Contention State Aware Dynamic Optimizer for Accelerator Collective Communication Libraries
item.description: arXiv:2611.10984v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collective Communication Libraries (CCL) are critical for large-scale distributed AI/ML training, yet their configurations are determined by static heuristics that do not account for real-time network conditions. Our empirical study shows that these heuristics perform near-optimally in contention-free environments, but degrade substantially under background traffic. To address this, we present a cooperative multi-agent run-time optimizer for accelerator collective communication. Our approach employs a two-agent architecture: (i) detector- a Long Short Term Memory(LSTM) recurring neural network fed classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test that distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes; and (ii) selector- a configuration selector built on a Dueling Double DQN (D3QN) with Conservative Q-Learning that adapts configuration parameters in response. We implemented this dynamic tuner over NCCL, a widely used CCL developed by NVIDIA. When evaluated on Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster, this dynamic tuning approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. We further evaluated it across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers, and recommendation architectures. Our multi-agent tuner approach delivers up to 65% speedups on Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric internode connectivity.
item.dc:creator: Rajat Bisht (Tennessee Technological University), Tevfik Kosar (University at Buffalo), Anthony Skjellum (Tennessee Technological University), Gene Cooperman (Northeastern University), MD S Q Zulkar Nine (Arkansas Tech University)

item.title: Advancements in Cloud-Native Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study of Reliability and Scalability across Cloud-Native, Edge-Native and AI-Enabled Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.11040v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cloud-native systems now extend to the network edge and host artificial-intelligence (AI) workloads, including AI agents, but evidence on their reliability and scalability is scattered and uneven. We report a PRISMA 2020 systematic mapping study with an evidence-graded synthesis. Five logged OpenAlex searches on 11 October 2026 covered cloud-native systems, edge AI, agentic AI for operations, reliability of agentic applications and physical AI; 189 records from an earlier exploratory search were added separately. After 301 duplicate removals and an automated peer-review venue rule, 4,611 records were screened against written criteria and a five-level relevance scale. The review includes 1,794 primary studies from 2017-2026 and 95 secondary studies, with every decision released in Dataset S1. Each primary study was assigned to a 13-category taxonomy and graded as simulation, prototype or testbed, production data, production deployment, or not determinable from the abstract. Of 1,003 studies with a determinable level, 66.2% used prototypes or testbeds, 18.0% simulations and 15.8% production data or deployments. A 93-study synthesis core, appraised from indexed abstracts, shows production deployments of cascading-failure prevention, trace- and graph-based root-cause analysis and predictive autoscaling, and production-trace evaluations of cold-start mitigation. Edge reliability and physical AI rely mainly on simulations and testbeds. AI-agent reliability uses tool-grounded diagnosis, explicit safety properties, trace-driven repair and workload-aware scheduling, while empirical studies show that agent frameworks remain fragile. Conclusions are limited to the documented corpus. The principal gaps are production evidence for edge-native systems, shared resilience benchmarks and dependable agentic operations.
item.dc:creator: Shrinivass Arunachalam Balasubramanian

item.title: GARP: Real-Time Generative Agents on Local Hardware in a Game Engine
item.description: arXiv:2611.11064v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative agents are game characters whose plans, conversations, and memories are written on the fly by a large language model (LLM). The original Generative Agents demonstration used cloud inference in a custom simulation. We present GARP, a platform for real-time generative agents inside Godot, and describe the Character Behavior System used in GARP 2. The complete loop runs on local hardware using a 3B-parameter open-weight model and no cloud service. Alongside the original planning, memory, and reflection, GARP gives each agent an emotion system driven by LLM appraisal, four graded personality axes drawn from the Big Five that set simulation parameters as well as prompt text, six needs whose urgency grows over time, and pairwise relationships updated after every conversation. The system narrows 50+ candidate actions to typically 3-8, constrains model responses with JSON schemas, and surfaces important memories in decision prompts. A layered optimization strategy (an adjustable game clock, decisions taken ahead of need, multi-tier caching, prompt compression, and fully asynchronous execution) keeps the game responsive while the model thinks. In a nine-scenario evaluation, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks. Both failures occurred in the birthday party scenario, where one guest omitted the event from their daily plan.
item.dc:creator: Piero Molino, Patrick John Chia, Federico Bianchi, Jonathan P. Chen, Paul Szerlip

item.title: LoMASA: A Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant with Confidence-Gated Delegation for B2B Quoting
item.description: arXiv:2611.11234v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frontline sales staff spend much of their day re-coordinating quotes after customers change quantities, ask for discounts or new payment terms, or costs move. We present LoMASA (Local Multi-Agent Sales Assistant), a training-free multi-agent system that runs entirely on one desktop computer. A 35B mixture-of-experts model (System-1) makes each decision in a single forward pass and reads its confidence from the probabilities of the answer options. A 27B dense model (System-2) writes customer replies and escalation briefs and is consulted when System-1 is unsure. Code computes every price, margin and option, and hard pricing rules cannot be overridden. On a test split of 500 simulated episodes with 1512 decisions built from public supply-chain data, the salesperson has to decide only 19.5% of decisions: 38.0% are settled automatically, with a median latency of 2.67 seconds, and 42.5% are escalated to a manager by the hard rules. On the automatically settled decisions LoMASA is as accurate as a rule baseline (0.894 vs.\ 0.894) and makes fewer commitments whose margin later falls below the floor (2.61% vs 4.53%); the price is additional escalations to the manager. Option probabilities are well calibrated without any training, unlike confidence stated in words by the same model. We also report where the design does not help: the 27B model rarely changes a decision.
item.dc:creator: Yu Liu, Xingbang Du

item.title: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.11266v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. Prior benchmarks isolate a single agent under prompt injection or score multi-agent attacks by their final output, leaving cross-session erosion of shared state out of scope. We introduce ErosionBench, an environment-grounded benchmark that executes such attacks and verifies alignment decay at the process level, scoring the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance with deterministic contracts, not output text. Each scenario is authored as a deterministic state graph before any prose is rendered, so every state change traces to a known cause. It spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms across 1,728 scenarios with matched benign controls, labeled against the OWASP Top-10 for LLM Applications, plus 198 image-based attacks, each paired with a text equivalent, so a defense must survive the same attack in either channel. Perimeter defenses suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work, so a low attack-success rate can conceal severe over-refusal. As a reference defense, we propose a calibrated Meta-Auditor pairing synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitoring; on a family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split it reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false-positive rate. Since it monitors trajectory, not surface content, its detection is channel-invariant: the strongest auditor flags image-delivered attacks about as reliably as their text equivalents (recall gap $\leq$2 points per model). Across GPT, Gemini, and Claude auditors, calibration keeps false positives low while recall tracks model capability, strongest for Claude.
item.dc:creator: Riya Bharathwaj, Akshara Prabhakar, Roshan Ram, Avni Kothari, Sarah Tan, Huan Wang, Silvio Savarese

item.title: ODSA: Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation
item.description: arXiv:2611.11621v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Test-time scaling improves the accuracy of a language model's answers by spending more computation at inference time. Established methods do so either sequentially, revising a single solution over several passes, or in parallel, generating several independent solutions and selecting among them. We present ODSA (Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation), an LLM-directed scaling framework in which an orchestrator LLM is given existing test-time scaling methods as actions --- discovery of a new independent solution, comparison of existing solutions to build a better one, and acceptance of a proposed answer, which triggers its verification --- and directs stateless workers to carry them out. The orchestrator does not solve the problem itself: it allocates computation, feeds the results of earlier actions into later ones, and takes every action from a single context, so that each decision is informed by everything tried before. On Humanity's Last Exam, ODSA improves accuracy by 4.7 to 18.0 points across three models over a single direct call to the model with no test-time scaling. On LiveCodeBench, where a single direct call already solves most problems, it improves accuracy by 0.6 to 14.0 points.
item.dc:creator: Macardle Meng, Haomin Zhang

item.title: PA-SaR: Perception-Aware Learning, Control, and Coordination for Multi-Robot Search and Rescue
item.description: arXiv:2611.11648v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.
item.dc:creator: Jocubas Dimsa, Maria Grouev, Filip Keerberg, Nicolas Laplagne, Tigo Schutgens, Sven Schoonebeek, Anahita Jamshidnejad

item.title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
item.description: arXiv:2611.11720v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.
item.dc:creator: Eyhab Al-Masri, Wenjun Yang

item.title: A Benchmark and Layered Evaluation Protocol for Evidence-Grounded Shared Belief Updating in Connected Robotics
item.description: arXiv:2611.11842v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Connected physical systems fuse observations from robots, IoT sensors, and edge-AI modules into a shared account of the world, yet most evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed the evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions, and justified its decision. We argue that shared reasoning in Connected Robotics should be evaluated as an evidence-to-belief trajectory, and introduce the Connected Robotics Evidence Graph (CREG) Benchmark to make that trajectory measurable. CREG comprises 350 deterministically generated scenarios across seven regimes (justified revision, belief preservation, relation association, contradiction onset and resolution, stale/delayed evidence, and source reliability), each exposing a normative posterior reference at every evidence prefix, validated by an independent log-odds checker and screened by a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata. Evaluating four open-weight instruction models and six transparent fusion baselines yields three findings. First, entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Second, deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), but an information-matched structured list outperforms the full graph and shuffling the graph does not hurt: relation content matters where required, while graph serialization confers no consistent advantage. Third, belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation cannot detect. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics, and analysis code are released for offline, hardware-free reproduction.
item.dc:creator: Ranulfo Bezerra, Kimitoshi Yamazaki

item.title: Competing Influence in LLM Populations: Budget Timing and Baseline Drift
item.description: arXiv:2611.11867v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When competing campaigns target a population of large language model (LLM) agents, observed opinion changes may reflect both campaign influence and changes that would occur without intervention. We study how the timing of campaign expenditure and the population's own evolution shape outcomes in a network of persona-conditioned LLM agents that exchange and revise opinions in natural language. A proponent and a challenger are tasked with generating opposing messages under equal delivery budgets, while a separate stance probe measures opinions without influencing the simulation. Across eight claims, we compare single-campaign and competitive conditions against matched no-campaign runs, and evaluate all nine combinations of early, sustained, and late spending on a reference topic. Baseline stance drift varies substantially across claims and, on some, accounts for a sizeable fraction of apparent campaign effects. After accounting for this drift, the direction of observed campaign-associated changes aligns more closely with the claim's epistemic standing than with the campaigner's assigned role. Uninfluenced populations also consistently lose stance diversity, demonstrating that directional opinion change and convergence are distinct phenomena. In networks with two opinion-segregated communities, campaigns primarily reduce differences between communities rather than diversity within them. LLM campaign agents do not always argue for their assigned positions, particularly when these conflict with established evidence. Finally, campaign outcomes depend on the opponent's expenditure schedule: unlike a matched numerical bounded-confidence population receiving interventions at the same times and locations, the LLM population exhibits a payoff structure with no pure-strategy equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Mehwish Nasim, Nicolas Fay

item.title: Modelling socio-economic effects of the pandemic in a metropolitan area
item.description: arXiv:2611.12270v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: One of the most notorious measures taken by authorities in every country trying to prevent the uncontrollable spread of the Covid 19 pandemic was to impose severe measures to diminish the mobility of people. In recent publications we proposed a mathematical model to address the consequences of these measures and to predict the infections under different scenarios, for various different countries. In this paper we extend the model, called the BTH--SEIRS-model, to deal with the reduction of mobility in an urban area. The chosen region was the densely-populated metropolitan area around Helsinki, the capital of Finland. This choice obeyed to the fact that there are precise data related to mobility from a mobile telephone company, and that this region was completely isolated from the rest of the country for a short period during the pandemic. We also used public transport data from railways and the accommodation occupation rates in the area of interest. We show that the BTH--SEIRS model is capable of simulating the real infection data as well as the mobility-related economic activity, exhibiting the main trends present in the three indicators used for comparison. Our calculations allow us to highlight the difference of the behaviour of the pandemic in a totally different spatial scale, and to discover the hidden factors that govern the behaviour of people who are forced to commute every day from home to work.
item.dc:creator: Jan E. Snellman, Rafael A. Barrio, Cecilia I. Ventura, Tzipe Govezensky, Kimmo K. Kaski, Maarit J. Korpi-Lagg

item.title: A Modular Perspective for Modeling MARL Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.12314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The growing complexity of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has fragmented the literature, obscuring underlying architectural choices behind diverse implementations. This fragmentation makes it difficult to evaluate critical modeling dimensions in isolation, identify how components affect the resulting system dynamics, and compare, reuse, or combine contributions across the literature. This paper proposes a modular perspective for modeling, analyzing, and implementing MARL systems. We decompose them into eight functional modules: agents, environments, learning, reward modeling, training and execution modes, communication, modeling of other agents, and evaluation criteria. For each module, we clarify its role and review representative approaches. We instantiate this decomposition in MARLKIT, a framework whose modules are explicit and interchangeable. MARLKIT demonstrates how the proposed perspective supports transparent experimental assumptions and the controlled variation and combination of MARL mechanisms. Experiments illustrate its ability to prototype, compare, reuse and combine modules while making differences between configurations explicit. Overall, the paper provides a structured perspective on MARL modeling and implementation, offering a common language for making modeling choices explicit, supporting clearer descriptions of MARL approaches, and supporting more controlled experimentation through the systematic isolation and combination of MARL mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Tiziano Maisonhaute, Jean-Christophe Souli\'e, Fabien Michel

item.title: Teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.12545v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.
item.dc:creator: Goran Mitevski

item.title: LAMaS: A Modular Platform for Learning Low-Latency Multi-Agent Orchestration
item.description: arXiv:2601.10560v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In a multi-agent system (MAS), removing an expensive agent call can save tokens without making the answer arrive sooner: latency depends on the longest chain of dependent calls. We present Latency-Aware Multi-agent System (LAMaS), a modular platform for learning low-latency orchestration. A framework can send a query to LAMaS and receive an answer and execution trace, or keep its own graph builder and use the platform's latency-optimized orchestration layer. During training, the layer gives operators on the critical path the greatest latency penalty while targeting a floor on expected accuracy. During inference, a lightweight controller uses partial results to decide whether to skip work that has yet to start. Across four benchmarks, LAMaS reduces end-to-end latency by over 50% relative to the evaluated learning-based MAS baselines while maintaining competitive or better accuracy. GDesigner and AgentDropout retain their graph builders and train the controller on their own traces; both achieve lower latency across the same benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Xi Shi, Mengxin Zheng, Qian Lou

item.title: Modelling Opinion Dynamics at Scale with Deep MARL
item.description: arXiv:2606.07487v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modelling opinion dynamics typically relies on hand-crafted local interaction rules to study emergent macroscopic phenomena such as consensus and polarisation. In contrast, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables agents to learn such behaviours directly by optimising simple rewards. To explore the potential of MARL for opinion dynamics, we introduce a GPU-accelerated consensus and truth-finding game that scales to populations of up to 1000 agents, comparable to many real-world social sub-networks. To prevent unrealistic conventions, we extend other-play to general-sum social interactions. We next validate our model on a subset of the Bluesky network by recovering agent importance structures from graph topology alone via a learned attention layer, finding that highly conforming populations most closely match human data. In large social media networks, such high levels of conformity significantly reduce collective accuracy and promote dishonest agents that lie to fit in. By contrast, small hunter-gatherer networks are less affected; here, conformity can even improve collective agreement. This suggests a mismatch between evolved human conformity heuristics and modern social media environments as a potential contributor to misinformation.
item.dc:creator: Lukas Seier, Brandon Kaplowitz, Sebastian Towers, Richard Bailey, Jakob Foerster

item.title: Rate-Aware Quantum-Inspired Trajectory Learning for Interference-Limited Multi-UAV Networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.25480v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Placing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as aerial base stations is non-convex and combinatorial, so practical methods first discretize the continuous airspace into a finite set of candidate positions---a uniform grid or clustering centroids---and optimize over that set. Built from Euclidean distance alone, the candidate set is channel-blind: it ignores line-of-sight probability and the co-channel interference that limits achievable rate under full frequency reuse. No optimizer can select a position the candidate set omits, so good locations the geometry missed are lost before the search begins. We propose Rate-Aware Quantum-Assisted Graph Condensation (RA-QAGC), a two-stage framework that makes the candidate set itself the object of optimization. The first stage constructs it by annealing a cost that embeds tier-weighted achievable rate, mean co-channel interference, and an explicit minimum-rate penalty, yielding a compact, mobility-feasible waypoint graph. The second stage learns trajectories over that graph with decentralized independent Q-learning agents, replacing a centralized joint-action table with one compact table per UAV. RA-QAGC improves priority-tier throughput by 21--54\% over seven baselines, including recent graph-neural and deep Q-network schemes, at no significant cost in aggregate throughput, and the margin widens as the fleet densifies. We additionally examine the quantum-inspired acceptance rule that recent aerial-networking work advocates, and report that its tunnelling floor confers no measurable advantage over classical simulated annealing at any fleet size tested, while annealing itself clearly outperforms greedy and random placement.
item.dc:creator: Khaoula Khaled, Muhammad Afaq, Zeeshan Kaleem

item.title: FlowMAS: Learning Multi-Agent Workflow Topology via Information-guided Generative Flow Network
item.description: arXiv:2609.37151v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated multi-agent systems offer clear advantages over manually designed ones in scalability and adaptability, but existing workflow topology methods still face important limitations. Search-based methods are often computationally expensive, textual-gradient-based methods rely on coarse-grained feedback, and existing generation-based methods are not well suited to discrete workflow topologies with complex dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose FlowMAS, a multi-agent workflow topology method based on Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets). FlowMAS models workflow generation as reward-guided flow over the topology space and introduces three components: a GFlowNet-based topology generation backbone, a curiosity-driven module for structure-aware exploration, and an information-guided optimization module for evaluating intermediate topologies. Concretely, the curiosity-driven module encourages exploration of structurally novel workflows, while the information-guided module measures both the information contribution and the communication efficiency of different operators to favor more informative and effective collaboration patterns. Experiments on six benchmark datasets with three LLM backbones show that FlowMAS consistently outperforms multiple baselines.
item.dc:creator: Haitao Wang, Chenjing Liang, Haipeng Zhang, Jiawei Hu, Sicheng Wang, Songzhu Mei, Chenglu Wen, Siqi Shen, Cheng Wang

item.title: Distributed Learning of $\alpha$-Potential Functions in Strategic Multi-agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.05516v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of computing the tightest \(\alpha\)-potential approximation of a general-sum game over continuous action spaces, within a prescribed class of potential functions and when each player has access only to its own utility function. The difficulty is twofold: the approximation error involves a worst-case search over an infinite set of unilateral deviations, and the required utility information is distributed across players. For a linear-in-parameters potential class, we use an exact finite-tuple reformulation that separates the problem into a global outer search over deviation tuples and distributed convex inner problems. We develop a primal--dual inner oracle tailored to this structure and establish a uniform one-sided accuracy guarantee. This oracle can be combined with global outer search to obtain an end-to-end guarantee on the outer optimization error. We also develop a projected zeroth-order outer method as a computationally lighter alternative for higher-dimensional problems. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy--computation tradeoff between the two outer-search methods and show that the proposed optimization framework can improve upon analytical \(\alpha\)-potential constructions.
item.dc:creator: Yifei Chen, Chinmay Maheshwari

item.title: When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.41132v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, self-interested drivers also make A a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each. Rebalancing policies that perform equally well under full compliance can thus show opposite results under mandatory disclosure. The study offers a framework to evaluate such policies under the new requirement and is, to our knowledge, the first to do so with LLM agents.
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Wang, Andres Fielbaum

item.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2611.01728v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.
item.dc:creator: Zerui Chen, Qinggang Zhang, Qichuan Liu, Zhishang Xiang, Zhimin Wei, Yunbo Tang, Zhuo Li, Jinsong Su, Zhihong Zhang

item.title: AIM: Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate for Multimodal LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.08950v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) improves reasoning on multimodal tasks, but its accuracy and token efficiency depend on how agents interact during debate. A largely overlooked design choice is which interaction modalities agents use to exchange evidence. Existing methods rely on fixed text- or graph-based interaction, which fails to convey fine-grained multimodal evidence and thus degrades accuracy while inflating token cost due to verbose descriptions. To address this, we propose Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate (AIM), an adaptive routing framework that dynamically selects the optimal modality combination for inter-agent interaction in multimodal MAD. Beyond text and graph, AIM introduces task-dependent modality interaction, where agents exchange targeted regions of interest from the task-specific multimodal input, such as image regions, audio segments, or spatio-temporal video clips. To determine the best combination for each instance, AIM first generates a structured baseline response and extracts interpretable routing features that capture which evidence the instance requires, how confident the baseline agent is, and how much new evidence each modality would add beyond the baseline response. A lightweight router then uses these routing features to select a modality combination that avoids both under-fusion (i.e., agents miss decisive evidence) and over-fusion (i.e., redundant modalities inflate token cost) risks. Across eight benchmarks spanning three multimodal task families, AIM achieves the highest accuracy. Combining modalities improves accuracy by up to 6.4% over the best single-modality baseline, and adapting the combination per instance adds up to 4.2% over the most accurate fixed combination of each benchmark with up to 53.4% fewer tokens.
item.dc:creator: Wei Fan, JinYi Yoon, Bo Ji

item.title: Implicit Credit Learning for Sparse-Reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2509.21828v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a cooperative team receives feedback only at the end of an episode, a single outcome must guide many agents' earlier actions. Learning a dense team reward helps, but its decomposition does not automatically give each agent a useful policy update. We introduce IMAP, an online method that fits a shared Q/V reward model by comparing completed episodes according to their observed terminal outcomes. Local Q/V residuals provide agent-specific rewards; the same normalized weights combine them for a centralized critic and scale local advantages for decentralized PPO actors. We characterize when these local updates follow the learned team objective. With full returns and frozen reward heads, a sharp bound relates their gradient error to variation in future Q/V compatibility; an exact identity identifies additional continuation terms for general GAE. In experiments with terminal-only feedback, IMAP's local-actor configuration attains the highest reported mean among the compared methods on all nine SMACv2 scenarios and four MAMuJoCo tasks, and on two of three SMACLite scenarios. Controlled relay interventions confirm the predicted changes in actor credit while holding the learned team reward fixed. The gradient result concerns the fitted objective; benchmark returns measure performance on the original task outcomes.
item.dc:creator: The Viet Bui, Tien Mai, Hong Thanh Nguyen

item.title: Multi-Agent Conditional Diffusion Planning for Decentralized Wireless Resource Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2510.22969v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In wireless communication systems, efficient and adaptive resource allocation is essential for enhancing overall Quality of Service (QoS). Compared with conventional Model-Free Reinforcement Learning (MFRL), Model-Based RL (MBRL) first learns a generative world model for subsequent planning, enabling more stable training through the reuse of historical experience. However, deploying MBRL in large-scale wireless networks remains challenging due to high-dimensional stochastic dynamics, strong inter-agent cooperation, and stringent communication constraints. To overcome these challenges, we propose a Multi-Agent Conditional Diffusion Model Planner (MA-CDMP) for decentralized communication resource management. Following the Decentralized Training with Decentralized Execution (DTDE) paradigm, MA-CDMP models each communication node as an autonomous agent and employs Diffusion Models (DMs) to capture environment dynamics. An inverse dynamics model is further incorporated to guide action generation, improving sample efficiency and policy scalability. Moreover, to efficiently approximate large-scale agent interactions, we introduce a Mean Field (MF) mechanism to assist the classifier in conditional DMs. This mitigates inter-agent non-stationarity and enhances cooperation with minimal communication overhead. We further establish an upper bound on the distributional approximation error induced by MF-based diffusion generation, guaranteeing convergence stability and reliable modeling of multi-agent stochastic dynamics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MA-CDMP consistently outperforms existing MARL baselines in terms of average reward and QoS metrics, showcasing its scalability and practicality for real-world wireless network optimization.
item.dc:creator: Kechen Meng, Sinuo Zhang, Rongpeng Li, Yansha Deng, Chan Wang, Zhifeng Zhao

item.title: Beyond Reasoning: RL-Policy Guided LLM Inference for Efficient Strategy in Liar's Poker
item.description: arXiv:2511.03724v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI researchers have long focused on poker-like games as a testbed for environments characterized by multi-player dynamics, imperfect information, and reasoning under uncertainty. While recent breakthroughs have matched elite human play at no-limit Texas hold'em, the multi-player dynamics are subdued: most hands converge quickly with only two players engaged through multiple rounds of bidding. In this paper, we present Solly, the first AI agent to achieve elite human play in reduced-format Liar's Poker, a game characterized by extensive multi-player engagement. We trained Solly using self-play with a model-free, actor-critic, deep reinforcement learning algorithm. Solly played at an elite human level as measured by win rate (won over 50% of hands) and equity (money won) in heads-up and multi-player Liar's Poker. Solly also outperformed large language models (LLMs), including those with reasoning abilities, on the same metrics. Solly developed novel bidding strategies, randomized play effectively, and was not easily exploitable by world-class human players. In one extension, when Solly's policies were provided to LLMs as a domain-specific guide for inference, LLM performance improved and token costs decreased. This result suggests that low-cost RL agents can be used to boost LLM efficiency and reasoning capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Richard Dewey, Janos Botyanszki, Ciamac C. Moallemi, Andrew T. Zheng

item.title: Bench-MFG: A Benchmark Suite for Learning in Stationary Mean Field Games
item.description: arXiv:2602.12517v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rise of Mean Field Games (MFGs) has fostered a growing family of algorithms designed to solve large-scale multi-agent systems. However, the field currently lacks a standardized evaluation protocol, forcing researchers to rely on bespoke, isolated, and often simplistic environments. This fragmentation makes it difficult to assess the robustness, generalization, and failure modes of emerging methods. To address this gap, we propose a comprehensive benchmark suite for MFGs, focusing on the discrete-time, discrete-space, stationary setting. We introduce a taxonomy of problem classes, ranging from no-interaction and monotone games to potential and dynamics-coupled games, and provide prototypical environments for each. Furthermore, we present MF-Garnets, a method for generating random MFG instances to facilitate rigorous statistical testing. We benchmark a variety of learning algorithms across these environments, including a novel population-based approach (MF-PSO). To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark for MFGs.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Magnino, Jiacheng Shen, Matthieu Geist, Olivier Pietquin, Mathieu Lauri\`ere

item.title: Convergence of Byzantine-Resilient Gradient Tracking via Probabilistic Edge Dropout
item.description: arXiv:2604.00449v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study distributed optimization over networks with Byzantine agents that may send arbitrary adversarial messages. We propose Gradient Tracking with Probabilistic Edge Dropout (GT-PD), which combines a universal self-centred projection that clips incoming messages to a radius-$\tau$ ball around the receiver with a fully decentralized probabilistic dropout rule driven by a threshold-gated, dual-metric trust score in the decision and tracking channels. These identity-free defences bound adversarial perturbations while preserving doubly stochastic mixing. The projection preserves the honest network average exactly in every realization, even when honest messages are clipped. Under complete Byzantine isolation ($p_b=0$), GT-PD converges linearly to a neighbourhood of order $\alpha\sigma^2/(\mu n_{\mathcal H})$ plus higher-order network terms, matching centralized stochastic gradient descent to first order in the step size. We also give a radius computable from problem data that ensures honest messages remain unclipped with high probability. Under partial isolation ($p_b>0$), a leaky variant, GT-PD-L, controls accumulated tracking perturbations and converges linearly to a bounded neighbourhood governed by stochastic variance and the clipping-to-leak ratio, under explicit conditions on the step size, leak, and aggregate Byzantine mixing weight. With two-tier dropout and $p_h=1$, Byzantine isolation adds no variance to honest consensus dynamics. MNIST experiments under Sign Flip, ALIE, and Inner Product Manipulation attacks show that GT-PD-L outperforms coordinate-wise trimmed mean by up to 4.3 percentage points under stealth attacks.
item.dc:creator: Amirhossein Dezhboro, Fateme Maleki, Arman Adibi, Erfan Amini, Jose E. Ramirez-Marquez

item.title: Measuring What Tool-Using LLM Agents Actually Do: Structured Validation, Causal Error Propagation, and Fabricated Tool Use
item.description: arXiv:2604.16706v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tool-using agents built on large language models (LLMs) are usually scored by comparing the final answer with a reference text, using a string heuristic or an LLM judge. This is unreliable when the references describe the task rather than its answer. We replace it with a deterministic validator that checks the tools called, the executed parameters, the resulting state, and whether the values in the answer are supported by the correct tool observations. We re-scored 33,583 traces from 13 agents on simulated calendar, weather, medical and retail tools. The simulator reproduced all 10,396 logged observations, and the gold observations supported the validator in 16 of 18 disagreements with a three-annotator majority (the annotators in none). The instrument changes conclusions: on the same 306 traces, Gemini-2.0-Flash scores 63.4% under the substring heuristic and 5.6% under the validator. In a paired design (same task and model, with and without one schema-valid wrong argument injected into the first tool call), the error rate rises from 52.4% to 74.5% (+22.0 percentage points, 95% CI 18.4-25.5; 1,085 pairs, 7 models), and by 44.7 points (38.4-51.0) where the corrupted call executed without errors. An LLM-judge ensemble estimates +2.5 points on the same pairs. Agents also report tool results without executing any call, in 0-42.5% of traces depending on the model (rule-based lower bounds), largely because the harness accepts an action and a final answer in one completion. A rule-based runtime monitor costs about 7 microseconds per trace but reduces wrong answers mainly by abstaining.

item.title: Independent Learning of Nash Equilibria in Partially Observable Markov Potential Games with Decoupled Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2605.06377v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Nash equilibrium learning in partially observable Markov games (POMGs), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which agents cannot fully observe the underlying state. Prior work in this setting relies on centralization or information sharing, and suffers from sample and computational complexity that scales exponentially in the number of players. We focus on a subclass of POMGs with independent state transitions, where agents remain coupled through their rewards, and assume that the underlying fully observed Markov game is a Markov potential game. For this class, we present an independent learning algorithm in which players, observing only their own actions and observations and without communication, jointly converge to an approximate Nash equilibrium. Due to partial observability, optimal policies may in general depend on the full action-observation history. Under a filter stability assumption, we show that policies based on finite history windows provide sufficient approximation guarantees. This enables us to approximate the POMG by a surrogate Markov game that is near-potential, leading to quasi-polynomial sample and computational complexity for independent Nash equilibrium learning in the underlying POMG.
item.dc:creator: Philip Jordan, Maryam Kamgarpour

item.title: SkillOps: Managing LLM Agent Skill Libraries as Self-Maintaining Software Ecosystems
item.description: arXiv:2605.13716v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skill libraries for multi-step tasks, yet these libraries can accumulate persistent defects as skills are added, reused, patched, and linked to changing dependencies. We call this failure mode skill technical debt: library-level defects that may not break a single skill locally but can harm future retrieval, composition, and execution. Existing skill-based agents mainly focus on task-time retrieval, planning, and repair, while library-time maintenance remains underexplored. We propose SkillOps, a method-agnostic plug-in framework for maintaining skill libraries. SkillOps represents each skill as a typed Skill Contract (P, O, A, V, F), organizes skills with a Hierarchical Skill Ecosystem Graph, and diagnoses library health across utility, compatibility, risk, and validation dimensions. Given a raw skill library, SkillOps produces a maintained library that can be used by existing retrieval or planning agents without changing their internal code. On ALFWorld, SkillOps achieves 79.5 percent task success as a standalone agent, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.8 percentage points with no additional task-time large language model calls. As a plug-in layer, it improves retrieval-heavy baselines by 0.68 to 2.90 percentage points. The current rule-based maintenance implementation uses nearly zero library-time large language model calls or tokens, showing that skill-library maintenance can be added as a low-overhead architectural layer.
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Song, Hongji Pu, Liang Zhao

item.title: Scale-Dependent Collective Adaptation in Self-Amending LLM Societies: A Cross-Family Study of Emergent Governance
item.description: arXiv:2605.17510v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study group decision-making in artificial societies where the rules of play are themselves subject to collective amendment. Using the self-amending game Nomic, we compare multiple scales across two LLM families and find that collective adaptation does not improve monotonically with model size. Instead, both families exhibit a narrow mid-scale regime that supports sustained rule adoption, diverse amendments, and balanced consensus. Smaller models tend to remain rule-inert, whereas larger models often converge on restrictive voting patterns, and heterogeneous mixed-size groups collapse into veto-driven gridlock. These cross-scale contrasts persist under temperature perturbations and under a shift from unanimity to majority voting, although latent-state structure varies by family and scale. Hidden-state divergence alone does not explain collective performance: high representational divergence can coincide with poor behavioural outcomes. Linear probes reveal regime-selective coupling between latent vote-predictive signals and collective behaviour, but decodability is necessary rather than sufficient for adaptive play. Overall, the recurring regularity is non-monotonicity, not the particular scale at which the optimum appears. Self-amending games therefore provide a controlled testbed for studying collective adaptation in artificial societies beyond raw model scale.
